newsitem.title: ZAIRE: U.N. airlift of Rwandan refugees from Zaire starts.
newsitem.headline: U.N. airlift of Rwandan refugees from Zaire starts.

text.p: A U.N. airlift of Rwandan refugees home from Zaire began in earnest on Wednesday as rebels shrugged off President Mobutu Sese Seko's reluctance to hold talks at sea.
The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR said 186 unaccompanied refugee children left Kisangani city for Rwanda's capital on an Ilyushin plane and 50 refugees would soon leave for Gisenyi, Rwanda.

"This is the start of the airlift which we hope will break the logjam and get these refugees home," said UNHCR spokesman Peter Kessler. But officials said a fuel shortage in Uganda meant two more Ilyushins could not join flights on Wednesday.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila gave U.N. agencies 60 days from Thursday to return all Rwandan refugees to Rwanda but told U.S. envoy Bill Richardson on Tuesday he was ready to be flexible.

The airlift was first delayed by rebel fears that a cholera outbreak could spread to local villagers and then by an attack on refugee camps by local villagers and rebels last week that scattered tens of thousands of refugees into forests.

U.N. officials have said it is impossible to repatriate all 100,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees south of Kisangani and another 250,000 unaccounted for in Zaire within 60 days even with full rebel cooperation.
Richardson, U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, said earlier in Kisangani he still hoped to salvage a face-to-face meeting between Kabila and Mobutu.
"I have a lot to talk to Mr Mobutu about," said Richardson, who before leaving Kisangani for the capital Kinshasa visited a camp for the Hutu refugees waiting to be flown to Rwanda.
"We still have a possibility of other venues, even this (sea) venue...we will just have to wait and see," he added.

Richardson questioned the human rights record of the rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire and said the world wanted an investigation of allegations of a massacre of refugees by Zairean villagers and rebels last week.

"The international community in judging the Alliance will be considering many things," he said. "Will it be a fair Alliance, a democratic Alliance? Will it have a proper record when it comes to human rights?"
"So far we are disappointed. They must do better."

In Luxembourg on Tuesday, European Union commissioner Emma Bonino accused Kabila's forces of trying to wipe out the Hutu refugees, suspected by rebels of having taken part in the 1994 genocide in Rwanda of about 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates.
Although a U.S. diplomat said Mobutu had refused talks on a South African ship, Mobutu's son and spokesman Nzanga Mobutu declined to rule out face-to-face talks off the coast of Zaire.
A senior aide to Kabila in Lubumbashi city said he did not care if Mobutu refused to meet. Rebel foreign policy strategist Bizima Karaha said: "No change in venue will be accepted by us."

The aide in Zaire's second city told Reuters the rebels were consolidating a push toward Kinshasa from Kikwit, 390 km (240 miles) east of Kinshasa, to eject Mobutu. The rebels have seized more than half of Zaire and captured Kikwit town on Tuesday.
"We lose nothing by not meeting Mr Mobutu. If anything we have bent backwards too much for the man given our military superiority on the ground," he said.
"We are more than happy to take the war to Kinshasa and end Mobutu's arrogance. In fact, our forces are consolidating their approach towards Kinshasa. He must know it is the end game."
South Africa on Wednesday urged both sides to negotiate.
U.N. aid workers in Kisangani said the refugees who started flying home to Rwanda on Wednesday were unexpectedly delivered by the rebels to the northeastern capital aboard a train.
The U.N. World Food Programme said it sent a train with 113 tonnes of food on Wednesday back to Biaro camp, 41 km (25 miles) to the south, the first shipment to the area since April 21.
